title: How widespread is algorithmic management in workplaces?
date_evidence: HOW WIDESPREAD IS ALGORITHMIC MANAGEMENT IN WORKPLACES? (c) OECD 2025 -- oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2025/12/how-widespread-is-algorithmic-management-in-workplaces_d1e62812/cda7a114-en.pdf
key_claim: An OECD employer survey of more than 6,000 firms across the US, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and Japan finds algorithmic management (software to instruct, monitor or evaluate workers) is already near-universal: 90% of US firms and an average of 79% in the European countries surveyed have adopted at least one such tool (40% in Japan). 60% of managers say decision quality has improved, but two-thirds flag major risks, led by unclear accountability (28%), inability to follow the tools' logic (27%) and inadequate protection of worker health (27%); worker surveys show reduced satisfaction, higher stress, lower trust and greater job insecurity.
notes: Structural anchor (3-6 month band). Canonical primary prevalence source AND the source of the counter-evidence (managers report improved decisions) and the worker-harm evidence.

title: AI Act: regulatory framework, high-risk classification and application timeline
date_evidence: Last update 11 May 2026 ... a political agreement was reached on 7 May 2026 ... Rules for systems used in certain high-risk areas -- including biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, migration, asylum and border control -- will apply from 2 December 2027.
key_claim: The EU AI Act classifies AI tools for employment and management of workers (e.g. CV-sorting recruitment software) as high-risk, subject to strict obligations including human oversight, risk and data-quality management and transparency. Following the 7 May 2026 political agreement on the AI 'omnibus' simplification, the binding obligations for high-risk systems in employment will apply from 2 December 2027 (and 2 August 2028 for systems embedded in products), rather than the original 2 August 2026; the Act's transparency rules still take effect in August 2026.
verbatim_quote: AI tools for employment, management of workers and access to self-employment (e.g. CV-sorting software for recruitment)
notes: Tier 1 EU primary. Anchors the high-risk classification and the deferral of binding obligations to December 2027 -- the governance-gap core of the signal.

title: Algorithmic control: How digital surveillance is shaping online platform work in Europe
key_claim: A Eurofound-ELA survey of almost 4,000 online platform workers across 15 EU Member States finds intensive algorithmic surveillance: about 78% experience time tracking, 67% communications monitoring and 53% screen/keystroke monitoring; 43% operate under a 'comprehensive control' regime; and the most cognitively demanding, highly skilled tasks (software developers, AI-services workers, technology consultants) face the most intensive algorithmic management -- which Eurofound frames as a test case for algorithmic management in traditional employment.
verbatim_quote: professional work carried out through online labour platforms is a test case for the use of algorithmic management systems in traditional employment contexts, where they are increasingly being deployed
notes: Tier 2 EU research agency. Leading-edge evidence on surveillance intensity; platform-work scope noted in body.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Human Resources in the EU: a 2026 Legal Overview
date_evidence: Client Alert | 6 min read | 02.24.26. The year 2026 marks a major regulatory turning point for European companies using or considering the use of artificial intelligence in their human resources (HR) processes.
key_claim: Many HR AI tools are likely high-risk under the AI Act -- automated candidate selection, performance evaluation, workplace monitoring, turnover prediction and decisions on promotion or termination -- triggering obligations including mandatory human oversight, transparency and prior information/consultation of employee representatives under Article 26(7); deployer non-compliance can draw fines up to EUR 15 million or 3% of global turnover. The Digital Omnibus proposes making high-risk deadlines conditional on harmonised standards, pushing application to as late as December 2027 or August 2028.
notes: Tier 3 law-firm alert. Source for the concrete HR high-risk categories, penalties, Article 26(7) worker-consultation duty and the deferral mechanics.

title: How a hiring algorithm is audited can disguise bias, study finds (Stanford 'algorithmic monoculture' study)
key_claim: A Stanford study of 4 million job applications screened by a single vendor algorithm (Pymetrics) across 156 employers and 11 sectors found clear racial disparities -- 26% of Black applicants' and 15% of Asian applicants' applications were directed to positions that adversely impacted them -- and a 10% systemic rejection rate; crucially, the vendor's previously published aggregated audits had shown no measurable bias, which only disaggregated analysis revealed. More than 90% of employers use some form of automation to filter or rank applicants (2025 WEF estimate), and an 'algorithmic monoculture' means a few shared vendor models can lock individuals out across many employers at once.
notes: Tier 3 journalism reporting a Stanford study. Source for the bias / audit-can-disguise-bias / monoculture evidence.

title: Half of current customer service jobs will be lost to AI by 2030, Forrester predicts (with Gartner counter-view)
key_claim: Forrester predicts AI will halve customer-service jobs by 2030, concentrated in high-volume, low-complexity roles; but Gartner counters that headcount cuts are 'the exception, not the rule' and that half of organisations planning severe AI-driven contact-centre cuts will drop those plans by 2027 -- much reduction is expected to come through attrition rather than layoffs.
verbatim_quote: Headcount cuts are the exception, not the rule
notes: Tier 3. Provides stakes and a sourced counter-view (Gartner) that the AI-replaces-workers narrative is overstated.

title: How Job Seekers Use AI to Research Employers Report 2026
date_evidence: PRESS RELEASE FROM PERCEPTIONX June 1, 2026 ... based on 306 respondents across seven countries
key_claim: A PerceptionX survey of 306 job seekers across seven countries finds AI now mediates both sides of the hiring relationship: 96% of AI-using job seekers use AI to research employers, 82% report AI changed their mind about pursuing a role, and 77% would delegate part or all of their job search to an AI agent -- directional evidence that AI is becoming embedded across the hiring funnel, not just on the employer side.
notes: Tier 4 vendor survey, directional only. Shows AI saturating the candidate side of hiring; corroboration, not anchor.
